title: Sandoz: medicines, dyes and Ovomaltine from Basel
what: Sandoz is one of the three big chemical and drug companies of Basel; its neighbour and rival is Ciba-Geigy. It makes medicines, dyes and chemicals, seeds and farm chemicals, and through Wander, merged in 1967, nutrition products such as Ovomaltine and Isostar.
why: The listing beat: a diversified Basel group whose future lies in one drug still in trials, cyclosporin. It ends in the Novartis merger of 1996.

title: Sandoz's cyclosporin used in a liver transplant
what: On 9 March Thomas Starzl in the United States used Sandoz's experimental drug cyclosporin in a liver transplant. Sandoz scientists discovered on 31 January 1972 that the substance, isolated from a soil fungus, damps the immune system, and doctors in Cambridge led by Roy Calne have shown promise in kidney transplants. It is still in trials.
why: The seed of Sandimmun, the drug that makes Sandoz's 1980s.

title: Sandoz profit up 17%, but the Basel parent stagnates
what: On 30 April Sandoz reported 1980 sales up 10.3% to 4.9 billion francs and group profit up 16.8% to 202 million, which management called satisfactory. Dyes weakened in the second half as the economy cooled, while pharmaceuticals and seeds grew faster. The annual report welcomes the end of the franc's overvaluation, which had hurt Swiss exporters; the Basel parent company itself is stagnating.
why: A snapshot of the pre-Sandimmun conglomerate: modest growth, dyes tied to the business cycle, and the strong franc as a constant worry for Swiss exporters.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 2 May 1981, p. 21 ('«Befriedigendes» Sandoz-Konzern-Ergebnis'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1981-05-02.pdf (read 2026-10-03)

title: America approves Sandimmune
what: The US Food and Drug Administration approved cyclosporin for clinical use on 14 November; Sandoz sells it as Sandimmune (Sandimmun in Switzerland). It damps the immune system so that the body does not reject a transplanted organ.
why: The drug that turns Sandoz into a pharma growth story; the share more than doubles from here to 1987.

title: Schweizerhalle: fire at a Sandoz warehouse poisons the Rhine
what: In the early hours of 1 November a fire destroyed a Sandoz warehouse at Schweizerhalle near Basel holding about 1,350 tonnes of pesticides and other farm chemicals. Firefighting water carried the chemicals into the Rhine, turning it red and killing fish and eels from Switzerland through West Germany to the Netherlands; acrid smoke drifted over Basel. The cause of the fire is not known.
why: Sandoz's darkest moment and one of Europe's worst environmental disasters: the share fell 17% in francs (13% in dollars) in November. Sandoz later paid CHF 43 million in compensation plus CHF 10 million to a Rhine fund; the disaster led to Switzerland's ordinance on major accidents.

title: Sandoz and Ciba-Geigy to merge as Novartis
what: On 7 March Sandoz and Ciba-Geigy, Basel's old rivals, announced that they will merge into a new company called Novartis, the largest corporate merger ever; the two had combined sales of nearly $30 billion last year. Ciba-Geigy's chairman Alex Krauer is to be chairman and Sandoz's pharma chief Daniel Vasella chief executive. Sandoz's bearer share jumped from 1,126 to 1,384 francs in March, Ciba-Geigy's from 1,067 to 1,475.
why: The defining event of the Sandoz arc: +24% in a month (23% in francs) and the end of an independent Sandoz. The exchange terms were not confirmed in a source read.
